demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
At nineteen, she is one of the youngest stylists in the salon, quick with her hands and careful with other people's appearance in a way that makes clients trust her almost immediately. She stands for long hours under bright mirrors, talking lightly about hair color and split ends, but she lives with the feeling that one wrong move can ruin a life. That belief begins one humid evening about a year ago, after she finishes a shift and borrows her older cousin's motorbike to get food for her family.

She grows up in a close South Eastern Asian household where errands are shared without much discussion. She remembers being tired but in a good mood, still wearing a black salon T-shirt that smells faintly of hairspray and shampoo. The roads are crowded, familiar, full of people weaving around one another in the ordinary chaos she has known since childhood. She is turning at an intersection she has crossed many times when a boy on a bicycle comes into view too late. She brakes hard. There is the scream of tires, the sharp metal sound of impact, and then his body on the road.

What she remembers most clearly is not the collision itself but the moment after: the way everything goes silent inside her while everyone around her starts shouting. She sees blood near his head. Someone pulls her away from the bike. Someone else is yelling for help. She is kneeling and saying, "I'm sorry, I'm sorry," over and over, though she cannot tell if she is speaking out loud. At the hospital she learns he is seriously injured but alive. That fact does not comfort her in the way other people expect it to. In her mind, "alive" does not erase what she has done.

In the first weeks after the accident, she barely sleeps. When she closes her eyes she sees the bicycle appearing in front of her again, as if the moment is happening fresh each time. Sometimes she hears the sound before she sees anything, that abrupt crack of metal and pavement, and she wakes up sweating with her heart racing. During the day, any sudden movement in traffic makes her body jolt. She stops riding altogether and refuses even to sit behind someone else on a motorbike. Her boyfriend offers to escort her to work, but she becomes tense and snappish on the road, grabbing the seat and telling him to slow down, then apologizing and crying once they arrive.

At home, her family tries to reassure her that it was an accident, that crowded roads are dangerous, that she did not mean to hurt anyone. She nods because she knows they want her to agree, but privately she begins to feel set apart from them, as if they are talking about some other girl who deserves kindness. She searches social media for news about the injured boy. She imagines his family talking about her with hatred. She pictures his future altered because she was careless for one second. Even when there is no new information, she cannot stop checking.

The salon, which used to feel lively and easy, changes for her. The hairdryers are too loud. The clatter of dropped scissors makes her flinch. When clients move suddenly in the chair, she feels a burst of alarm before she can hide it. She still does precise work-sectioning hair, trimming around the face, mixing dye-but it takes more out of her than it used to, because so much of her attention goes into keeping herself steady. She avoids conversations about traffic, injuries, or anyone's children riding bikes. If a client mentions an accident they passed on the road, she goes quiet and lets a coworker take over the talking.

She used to enjoy the walk to the market after work with her boyfriend, stopping for iced drinks and street food. Now she chooses longer routes to avoid the intersection where the crash happened. If she cannot avoid it, her chest tightens before she even sees the corner. She scans the road constantly, judging distances, watching hands on handlebars, predicting every possible mistake. Sometimes she freezes at the curb, unable to step forward, embarrassed by how childish she feels. Her boyfriend squeezes her hand and tells her they can wait, but his patience sometimes makes her feel worse, as if she has become someone fragile he must manage.

She is also angry in ways that surprise her. When friends laugh loudly crossing the street or glance at their phones near traffic, she wants to shout at them. She thinks, You have no idea how fast everything can be destroyed. Then the anger turns inward. She calls herself stupid, reckless, dangerous. On difficult days she stands behind a client, catches her own reflection in the mirror, and feels a flash of disbelief that she still gets to have an ordinary life-folding towels, sweeping hair, answering messages from her boyfriend-when another person carries injuries because of her.

She still shows up to work on time. She still braids little cousins' hair at family gatherings and smiles in photos when asked. From the outside, much of her life looks intact. But she lives as if the worst moment of her life is never fully past, only waiting at the edge of her vision, ready to return whenever tires screech, whenever someone steps into the road too quickly, whenever her mind becomes quiet enough to remember.
